The town hired a man to move the bench six feet to the left.

There were reasons. The bench interfered with the sightline from the new municipal camera. Its present location encouraged congregation near the pharmacy entrance. A wheelchair user had complained—not about the bench, actually, but about the sandwich board beside it. Nevertheless, a report had been written, and the report recommended moving the bench.

The man’s name was Arthur. He arrived with a socket wrench, a cordless drill, and a sandwich wrapped in the paper his wife still bought in bulk, though she had been dead for eighteen months.

It was good paper. You couldn’t blame paper for outlasting somebody.

At nine fifteen he set two orange cones around the bench.

At nine seventeen a woman stepped between them and sat down.

“I’m moving this,” Arthur said.

“I won’t be long.”

She took a shoe box from her shopping bag and rested it on her knees.

Arthur checked the bolts. They had been painted over several times: green, black, green again. Municipal geology.

“You’ll need to get up eventually.”

“Everybody does.”

He decided not to pursue that.

Across the road, a boy in a butcher’s apron washed the shop window with a sponge. He was making it substantially wetter without making it noticeably cleaner. Arthur watched him for a while, then took out a wire brush.

The woman said, “Do you know anything about birds?”

“Not professionally.”

“This one flew into my conservatory.”

“Is it in the box?”

“Yes.”

“Alive?”

“That’s the question.”

Arthur stopped brushing.

“Have you opened it?”

“Of course I’ve opened it.”

“And?”

“It looked offended.”

“That’s usually promising.”

She lifted the lid half an inch. Arthur leaned over.

Inside, on a tea towel embroidered with lemons, sat a small brown bird. Its eyes were open. It appeared to be considering legal action.

“Probably stunned,” he said.

“That’s what my daughter said.”

“Your daughter know about birds?”

“She knows about most things since moving to Bristol.”

The woman lowered the lid.

Arthur managed to expose the head of the first bolt. It was a size he didn’t have.

This did not surprise him. In thirty-one years of maintenance work, he had rarely encountered a bolt that wanted to be removed.

“I’ll have to go to the van,” he said.

“I’ll watch your cones.”

When he returned, a second woman was standing beside the bench, looking into the box.

“Give it water,” she said.

“Don’t give it water,” said the first woman.

“My uncle kept pigeons.”

“This isn’t a pigeon.”

“Same principles.”

Arthur put the socket on the bolt and leaned. Nothing happened.

The second woman watched.

“You want some oil on that.”

“I do.”

“My uncle also worked on cars.”

“A versatile man.”

“He was, before the drinking.”

By ten o’clock the bench had acquired a small committee.

The pharmacist came out and said the bird should be kept somewhere quiet.

The butcher’s boy came across with a saucer.

A man waiting for the number eight said birds couldn’t smell, which nobody had asked about.

Arthur loosened the first bolt.

Everyone turned at the sharp metallic crack.

“That’s one,” he said, and found himself pleased by the attention.

He could not remember the last time four people had watched him accomplish something. At home, repairs had become private events. He had fixed the loose banister in February and still occasionally gripped it harder than necessary to appreciate the result.

The woman with the box introduced herself as June.

“Arthur.”

“I know. It’s on your shirt.”

He looked down. So it was.

At half past ten, he had removed three bolts. The fourth turned freely without rising.

“Nut underneath,” he said.

The committee accepted this diagnosis solemnly.

He lay down on the pavement.

Under the bench were two cigarette ends, a hair clip, and a coin pressed into a dark clot of chewing gum. Above him, people discussed whether the bird was a sparrow.

His wife would have known. Not because she knew birds, but because she would have gone into the library and come back with a book. She had trusted information that required walking somewhere.

Arthur fitted a spanner around the nut.

“Try it now,” he said.

No one moved.

“The wrench. On top.”

June held the box out to the pharmacist and bent over the bolt. Her first attempt slipped.

“Keep it level,” Arthur said.

“Like that?”

“That’s it.”

The bolt came free.

When he crawled out, June was holding it up by its clean silver end.

The butcher’s boy helped them carry the bench. Six feet to the left put it beside the library wall, where the paving sloped slightly. Arthur measured, drilled, and fitted new anchors while June sat on the wall with the box.

They were tightening the last bolt when something scratched inside it.

June took off the lid.

The bird remained still for a moment, then flew straight toward the pharmacy, swerved above the sandwich board, and disappeared over the roof.

Nobody had time to say anything useful.

The pharmacist returned to work with the empty saucer. The boy went back to his window. June folded the lemon towel and put it in her shopping bag.

Arthur collected the cones.

“Is it ready?” she asked.

He gave the bench a firm shake.

June sat down. After a moment, Arthur sat beside her and unwrapped his sandwich.

From its new position, the bench caught the sun. Unfortunately, it also offered a clear view of the butcher’s window.

“He’s missed a bit,” June said.

Arthur chewed.

“Several bits.”

Neither called across.
